content: Cost-benefit analysis (CBA) evaluates the monetary value of outcomes over time for all stakeholders involved in an intervention. These values are derived from the market prices and costs of tangible components, as well as estimated monetary values for intangible components that lack market values, using willingness-to-pay (WTP) techniques. Assigning monetary value to consequences makes CBA one of the most debated forms of economic evaluation. For example, when benefits are measured in terms of lives saved, assigning a monetary value to human life can provoke strong reactions. However, many digital health programs do not directly save lives but aim to improve healthcare delivery, making life valuation less relevant in these cases. Analysts often regard CBA as the methodological foundation for translating theory into a practical evaluation tool. The eHealth Impact (eHI) methodology is a version of CBA specifically applied to digital health evaluations. CBA is particularly useful when program managers and decision-makers need to compare intervention results with other projects competing for limited organizational resources. Cost-utility analysis (CUA) is a form of cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA) where outcomes are measured in terms of healthy years of life, often expressed as quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) or disability-adjusted life years (DALYs). For example, sending SMS reminders to healthcare providers to notify them of home births can be evaluated for cost-effectiveness in terms of increasing healthy years of life for newborns compared to not sending such messages. Cost-consequence analysis (CCA) examines the costs and consequences of an intervention without aggregating them into a single measure. For instance, a digital health intervention might be evaluated for its impact on the provision of perinatal care, the presence of trained attendants at births, vaccination rates for newborns, postnatal care for mothers, and improved education and development due to better health outcomes. Cost-minimization analysis (CMA) compares the relative costs of interventions that are assumed to have equivalent effects. For example, to provide tetanus toxoid immunizations to 1,000 pregnant women, one could compare the costs of using a community health worker to promote and refer women versus sending SMS reminders to encourage antenatal care attendance. The maturity stage of a digital health intervention determines the most appropriate evaluation activities. For early-stage solutions, such as pre-prototype or prototype phases, evaluations can help refine the program’s trajectory and avoid high-risk directions. Once the system is stabilized, evaluations are needed to advance testing and enable progression through different stages of evaluation. For interventions in advanced stages, such as integration or scale-up, predictive modeling may be used to estimate effectiveness and resource requirements for large-scale implementation. Evaluation methods should align with the maturity stage of the intervention. Early stages focus on feasibility, usability, and efficacy, while later stages emphasize effectiveness and scalability. Formative evaluations, typically conducted internally, aim to influence program design and implementation. Summative evaluations, often conducted by external entities, provide evidence to inform improvements, implementation, and expansion. Study designs should match the evaluation stage and evidence needs. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are the gold standard for efficacy or effectiveness evaluations when evidence is limited. However, quasi-experimental or observational designs may be more feasible when evidence is well-established or when RCTs are unethical or impractical. Hybrid study designs, which assess both clinical and implementation effectiveness, are emerging as valuable tools in implementation science. Evaluation methods should include a mix of quantitative, qualitative, economic, and financial approaches, depending on the selected inferences. Resources, timing, and audience needs will determine feasibility. Quantitative methods may include surveys, system-generated data, and disease surveillance, while qualitative methods may involve focus group discussions (FGDs), in-depth interviews (IDIs), and participant observation. Mixed-methods approaches combine quantitative and qualitative data to provide a comprehensive evaluation.
